title: Domain V: Leadership & Influence - Leadership & Influence - Professional Values & Ethics
subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: During the holiday season, a long-standing vendor delivers a basket of expensive chocolates to the procurement office. The agency policy allows for 'nominal gifts under $25,' but the basket's value is unknown. What is the most ethical action?
options: Accept the basket and share it with the entire department so no single person benefits.
Decline or return the gift to the vendor, explaining the agency's strict ethics policy.
Estimate the value, and if it seems under $25, accept it.
Accept the gift but ensure that vendor is not awarded the next contract to avoid favoritism.
questions.explain: Public procurement professionals must avoid even the appearance of impropriety. When in doubt regarding a gift's value or intent, the most ethical course of action is to politely decline or return it, citing agency policy.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: A buyer is assigned to evaluate bids for a new landscaping contract. The buyer realizes their sibling owns a landscaping company that has submitted a bid. What should the buyer do?
options: Evaluate the bids fairly and do not mention the relationship unless the sibling wins.
Disclose the conflict of interest to their supervisor and request to be removed from the evaluation process.
Review the sibling's bid and advise them on how to lower their price to be competitive.
Evaluate the bids but automatically disqualify the sibling's firm.
questions.explain: This is a clear conflict of interest. The buyer must disclose the relationship immediately to their supervisor and recuse themselves from the evaluation to maintain transparency, impartiality, and public trust.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: A City Council member privately asks the Procurement Manager to award a consulting contract to a specific local firm, citing the firm's recent campaign contributions. How should the Manager handle this political pressure?
options: Award the contract to the local firm to maintain a good relationship with the Council.
Inform the Council member that the award must be based on objective criteria and follow the statutory competitive process.
Alter the solicitation specifications so that only the local firm can meet the requirements.
Publicly denounce the Council member to the local media immediately.
questions.explain: Public procurement must remain impartial and independent of political pressure. The manager must professionally but firmly insist on adherence to established competitive processes and objective evaluation criteria.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: During an open, active solicitation, an end-user accidentally emails a vendor's proprietary technical schematic to a competing vendor. What is the immediate ethical obligation of the procurement professional?
options: Ignore the mistake, as it was the end-user's fault, not procurement's.
Cancel the solicitation immediately, document the breach, and assess how to proceed to ensure a fair playing field.
Quietly tell the competing vendor to delete the email.
Send the schematic to all other registered vendors to level the playing field.
questions.explain: When proprietary information is compromised during an active solicitation, the integrity of the process is fundamentally breached. The standard ethical response is to cancel, document, and restart the process to maintain fairness and protect vendor data.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: According to the NIGP Code of Ethics, accountability in public procurement primarily means:
options: Taking responsibility for one's actions and ensuring that decisions are justified, transparent, and defensible.
Ensuring the agency never exceeds its annual budget.
Defending the end-user's choice of vendor, regardless of the process used.
Making all purchasing data available on a public website in real-time.
questions.explain: Accountability is the obligation to take responsibility for actions, decisions, and policies. It ensures that procurement processes are justifiable, documented, and conducted in the public's best interest.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: A vendor who recently won a major IT contract invites the procurement director out for a 'celebratory lunch.' The vendor offers to pay. What is the most appropriate action for the director?
options: Accept the lunch, since the contract is already awarded and no competitive advantage can be gained.
Decline the invitation to avoid the appearance of a gratuity or favoritism.
Accept the lunch, provided the value is less than $100.
Attend the lunch, but bring an end-user as a witness to ensure discussions remain professional.
questions.explain: Accepting meals from vendors, even post-award, can create the appearance of impropriety, favoritism, or a conflict of interest for future contracts. It is best practice to decline such invitations.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: An end-user submits a specification for a fleet vehicle that includes the exact make, model, and proprietary features of one specific manufacturer, claiming it is the only vehicle that meets their needs. What is the ethical concern here?
options: It restricts open and fair competition by utilizing overly restrictive specifications.
It violates the agency's sustainability policy.
It forces procurement to use a cooperative contract.
It may result in the agency receiving too many bids.
questions.explain: Writing specifications that unnecessarily point to a single brand or manufacturer (restrictive specifications) limits open competition, violates the principle of fairness, and may prevent the agency from obtaining best value.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: While conducting a public bid opening, a buyer notices a mistake in a bidder's arithmetic on the pricing sheet. The unit price and total price do not match. What is the standard ethical approach to resolving this?
options: Reject the bid immediately as non-responsive.
Allow the bidder to alter their unit price after the opening to fix the total.
Apply the established agency policy regarding math errors, which typically dictates that the unit price governs.
Call the vendor during the bid opening and ask what they meant.
questions.explain: Impartiality requires consistent application of rules. Most procurement laws and policies dictate that in the event of an arithmetic discrepancy, the unit price prevails. Applying the written rule ensures fair treatment for all bidders.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: A newly hired buyer informs you that at their previous private sector job, it was customary to negotiate with bidders by revealing a competitor's price. They suggest doing this to save the agency money. How do you respond?
options: Agree, as saving taxpayer money is the ultimate goal of public procurement.
Explain that 'auctioning' or revealing competitor prices during negotiation is unethical and generally prohibited in public procurement.
Only reveal the competitor's price if the vendor signs a non-disclosure agreement.
Allow it only for formal Requests for Proposals (RFPs), but not Invitations to Bid (ITBs).
questions.explain: In public procurement, 'auctioning' (revealing competing prices or technical data during active negotiations) is unethical and compromises the integrity of the competitive process. It destroys vendor trust and is strictly prohibited.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: You witness a senior colleague accepting tickets to a sporting event from a vendor who is currently bidding on an agency project. What is your ethical obligation?
options: Mind your own business to maintain harmony within the procurement department.
Report the incident to the Chief Procurement Officer or appropriate ethics compliance officer.
Ask the vendor if they have any extra tickets for yourself.
Confront the vendor directly and demand they withdraw their bid.
questions.explain: Procurement professionals have a duty to uphold the integrity of the profession. Witnessing an unethical act, especially during an active solicitation (which compromises fairness), requires reporting to higher authority or an ethics officer.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: A 'perceived' conflict of interest is defined as a situation where:
options: An employee actively uses their position for direct financial gain.
An employee has no financial stake, but a reasonable person might believe the employee's judgment could be compromised.
A vendor sues the agency over a contract dispute.
An employee is related to another employee in a different government agency.
questions.explain: A perceived conflict of interest occurs when, even if no actual unethical act or financial conflict exists, the circumstances would lead a reasonable observer to question the employee's impartiality. Both perceived and actual conflicts must be avoided.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: A vendor offers 'free' sample materials to an agency department for testing. The department loves the material and submits a requisition specifying that brand. What is the ethical hazard?
options: The free materials create a bias and circumvent the competitive procurement process.
The materials might be of lower quality than advertised.
The vendor may claim tax deductions on the free materials.
There is no hazard; accepting free materials saves the agency money.
questions.explain: Accepting 'free' samples often leads to bias and the development of restrictive specifications, allowing the vendor to bypass fair competition. Free samples should only be accepted through a formal, managed testing program overseen by procurement.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: The anti-kickback act primarily prevents:
options: Contractors from subcontracting out more than 50% of a public works project.
Vendors from giving money or gifts to agency employees or prime contractors to improperly secure an award.
Agencies from returning unused inventory to a vendor for cash.
Agencies from utilizing federal funds for local projects.
questions.explain: Anti-kickback statutes are designed to deter the exchange of money, gifts, or anything of value given by a subcontractor or vendor for the purpose of improperly obtaining or rewarding favorable treatment in a contract.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: A procurement professional is reviewing an RFP document and notices that the evaluation criteria give 40% weight to 'past relationship with the agency.' Why is this ethically problematic?
options: It discriminates against new vendors and restricts fair and open competition.
It is difficult for the evaluation committee to score mathematically.
The weight should be no more than 10%.
Past performance can never be evaluated in an RFP.
questions.explain: While 'past performance' can be evaluated, heavily weighting 'past relationship with the agency' strongly favors incumbent vendors and creates an unfair barrier to entry for new, capable firms, stifling competition.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: Many jurisdictions have 'revolving door' policies. The primary ethical purpose of these policies is to:
options: Prevent employees from rotating between different internal agency departments.
Prohibit vendors from repeatedly submitting bids on different contracts.
Prevent former public officials from immediately working for vendors to leverage their insider knowledge or influence.
Ensure contracts are rotated among a list of pre-qualified vendors.
questions.explain: Revolving door statutes prevent former government employees from using relationships or insider knowledge acquired during public service to benefit private companies immediately after leaving public office.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: Transparency in public procurement is best demonstrated by:
options: Keeping all bid tabulations confidential to protect vendor pricing strategies.
Conducting evaluations entirely in closed sessions with no documentation.
Ensuring public access to procurement laws, procedures, solicitation documents, and award decisions.
Publishing the personal financial records of all procurement staff.
questions.explain: Transparency involves ensuring that procurement processes, rules, criteria, and outcomes are clear, predictable, and openly accessible to the public and vendor community, fostering trust.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: An agency receives a public records request for a winning vendor's RFP proposal. The proposal contains clearly marked trade secrets. How should the procurement official proceed ethically and legally?
options: Release the entire document, as all government documents are 100% public record.
Deny the public records request entirely.
Work with legal counsel to redact the valid trade secrets before releasing the rest of the document.
Contact the vendor and allow them to decide what should be released.
questions.explain: Procurement must balance transparency with the ethical/legal obligation to protect a vendor's proprietary trade secrets. Redacting legally protected information with the help of legal counsel ensures compliance with both obligations.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: When an error is discovered in a solicitation document right before the closing date, the ethical principle of fairness dictates that the buyer should:
options: Inform only the vendors who have already submitted bids.
Issue an addendum extending the closing date and detailing the correction to all prospective bidders.
Wait until bids are opened and allow vendors to adjust their prices.
Cancel the solicitation and never re-issue it.
questions.explain: Fairness dictates that all prospective bidders have equal access to correct information and adequate time to formulate their bids. Issuing an addendum and extending the deadline fulfills this ethical mandate.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: An ethical public procurement process requires that all prospective bidders have equal access to information. Which of the following violates this principle?
options: Hosting a public pre-bid conference and publishing the Q&A.
Answering questions from a single vendor over the phone without publishing the answer to others.
Using an electronic bidding system accessible via the internet.
Publishing solicitations in a local newspaper of general circulation.
questions.explain: Providing crucial information, clarifications, or answers to only one vendor gives them an unfair competitive advantage. All clarifications must be distributed to all potential bidders via a formal addendum.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: During an emergency declared by the agency head, procurement regulations allow for the waiver of competitive bidding. Ethically, the procurement professional should still ensure:
options: The contract is awarded to the agency's preferred vendor.
That the emergency purchase is limited to addressing the immediate threat and obtaining the best possible value under the circumstances.
The procurement bypasses all documentation requirements.
A 10-year contract is signed to prevent future emergencies.
questions.explain: Even during an emergency, procurement must act as a responsible steward of public funds. This means acquiring only what is necessary to mitigate the emergency and securing the best possible value given the time constraints.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: A department requires $15,000 of office equipment. The agency's formal bidding threshold is $10,000. The department head submits two separate requisitions for $7,500 each, two days apart, to the same vendor. This practice is:
options: An efficient use of small purchase procedures.
An unethical practice known as 'stringing' or 'split purchases' designed to circumvent competition thresholds.
Acceptable as long as there is enough money in the department's budget.
A legal loophole known as micro-purchasing.
questions.explain: Splitting a known requirement into multiple smaller transactions to avoid formal competitive bidding thresholds is an unethical and policy-violating practice known as 'stringing,' 'fragmenting,' or 'split purchases.'
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the ethical concept of 'Impartiality' in public procurement?
options: Treating all suppliers equally and evaluating offers objectively based solely on stated criteria.
Ensuring local businesses win at least 50% of all agency contracts.
Splitting contract awards equally among all submitting bidders.
Relying on end-users to select the vendor they prefer.
questions.explain: Impartiality means unbiased decision-making, where all suppliers are treated equally and fairly, and evaluation decisions are based strictly on objective criteria stated in the solicitation.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: A buyer is responsible for surplus asset disposal. The buyer wants to bid on a surplus agency laptop being auctioned to the public. Is this ethical?
options: Yes, as long as they pay the highest bid price.
Yes, if the buyer was not involved in declaring the item surplus.
No, because the buyer has insider information regarding the condition and value of the laptop.
No, unless they buy it through a third party.
questions.explain: Employees involved in the procurement or disposal process generally possess insider information regarding agency assets, creating an unfair advantage or a conflict of interest. Many agencies outright prohibit employees from bidding on agency surplus.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: You receive a formal bid package at 2:05 PM for a solicitation that officially closed at 2:00 PM. The vendor explains they were delayed by a severe traffic accident. Ethically and procedurally, you should:
options: Accept the bid because the delay was outside the vendor's control.
Reject the bid as late, timestamp it, and return it unopened.
Open the bid privately to see if it is significantly lower than others before deciding.
Ask the other bidders if they mind accepting a late entry.
questions.explain: Fairness and impartiality demand strict adherence to stated deadlines. Accepting a late bid compromises the integrity of the process and disadvantages vendors who adhered to the rules. Late bids must be rejected.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence

questions.q: A procurement professional notices that an evaluation committee member is consistently giving inexplicably low scores to one specific supplier. Ethically, the procurement professional should:
options: Alter the scores to balance them out.
Remove the supplier from the evaluation to appease the evaluator.
Discuss the scoring privately with the evaluator to ensure objective criteria are being applied without bias.
Ignore the scoring, as the committee member has final say.
questions.explain: The procurement professional acts as a facilitator and protector of the process's integrity. If bias is suspected, they must address the anomaly by ensuring the evaluator justifies their scores based solely on the published evaluation criteria.
questions.subject: Leadership & Influence
